name: Easy Reflection
baseline: nlohmann/json (JSON) and yaml-cpp (YAML); RapidJSON also measured
workload: Google Benchmark of serializing and deserializing one 2.9 KB user-profile document (benchmarks/data/boba_fett.json) to and from a reflected C++ struct, against nlohmann::json parse/dump, RapidJSON DOM parse/Writer and yaml-cpp load/emit of a generic node.
claimed_speedup: Per-operation times in microseconds read from the README chart (benchmarks/performance_chart.png, labelled Core i5): JSON serialization 2.8 vs nlohmann 9.3 (3.3x faster, derived from chart data); JSON deserialization 17.4 vs nlohmann 20.8 (1.2x), and 5.7 with the optional simdjson parser (3.6x); YAML serialization 3.4 vs yaml-cpp 331.8 (about 98x) and YAML deserialization 18.1 vs yaml-cpp 274.5 (about 15x), derived from chart data. RapidJSON on the same chart: 3.4 serialize, 7.4 parse. README text: 'JSON is faster than nlohmann json. Serialization is the same fast as rapid json, deserialization is a little faster with simdjson parser and more than twice slower without.'
hardware: Only 'Core i5' (image alt text); exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a clang-based code-generation step that parses [[er::reflect]] attributes and emits reflection code; C++17; native JSON, YAML 1.2 and a variable-length-integer binary format deserialize straight into typed objects (strings are converted to int, float and bool on load). Binary form is 61% of the JSON byte size (YAML 104%) per the repo's second chart, which is serialized size, not RAM.
caveats: Numbers exist only inside chart images (read from performance_chart.png); the README text gives no figures. Compiler, build type, flags and CPU model are not stated and benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt sets no optimisation flags. The benchmark compares different jobs: Easy Reflection builds a typed struct, while nlohmann, RapidJSON and yaml-cpp build or dump a generic DOM (the README notes the others do not convert strings to int, float or bool until accessed). One small 2.9 KB document only. The yaml-cpp ratios (about 98x and 15x) are implausibly large; README itself says 'if I did the benchmark right'. The README calls the project 'mostly a proof of concept' and tells users who want this in production to use glaze instead. Repository archived and read-only since 2026-08-20.

name: Expat
baseline: libxml2 (DOM parse; Expat measured in SAX mode)
workload: Wall-clock parse (median of 3 repetitions) of a generated synthetic XML file (sample_1mb.xml and sample_10mb.xml; the 1 MB file has 16,824 elements, nesting up to 22, attributes, entities, CDATA, comments and processing instructions), Expat as SAX events versus libxml2 building a DOM tree.
claimed_speedup: 1 MB: Expat (SAX) 11.525 ms, 86.9 MB/s vs libxml2 (DOM) 26.507 ms, 37.8 MB/s (2.3x faster, derived from page data); 10 MB: 121.381 ms, 82.4 MB/s vs 263.196 ms, 38.0 MB/s (2.2x, derived); peak RSS 7.38 vs 24.81 MiB at 1 MB and 25.44 vs 197.37 MiB at 10 MB. Earlier run of the same file, 1 MB: Expat (SAX) 15.495 ms, 64.6 MB/s vs libxml2 (DOM) 35.168 ms, 28.5 MB/s (2.3x, derived).
hardware: Intel Core i7-4850HQ (Haswell, 2013 laptop) at 2.3 GHz base clock, no turbo (stated for the cross-language parse tables)
tradeoffs: Non-validating, stream-oriented push parser in C with no tree, so memory stays near input size (7.38 MiB peak at 1 MB in the table above) but the caller must build any document structure; libxml2 additionally offers DOM, validation, XPath and HTML parsing.
caveats: Weak and contested evidence. The README of Expat itself says only 'Fast streaming XML parser' with no numbers. The figures come from the README of a competing 2026 project (libsimdxml, 0 stars, a C++23 port of the Rust simdxml) that lists Expat and libxml2 only as references; Expat and libxml2 versions, compiler and flags are not stated and the orchestrator script is under tmp/. The compared modes differ (Expat SAX vs libxml2 DOM), so this is not like-for-like. Like-for-like data points the other way: bemayer/xml-benchmark (report/index.html committed, run dated 2026-04-06, local runner, hardware not stated) has libxml2 SAX/Stream faster than Expat on every synthetic size, for example 1 MB 39.606 ms (617.6 MB/s) vs Expat 70.714 ms (345.9 MB/s), 10 MB 110.529 ms vs 145.468 ms, 100 MB 592.34 ms vs 933.022 ms, and 104.826 ms vs 234.468 ms in a result group labelled 'other'. Search snippets (pages blocked here, not verified) of older mailing-list posts disagree with each other: one has Expat about 10% faster than libxml2 on OSM data, another has libxml2 ahead by 30%. The sourceforge.net project page (expat.sourceforge.net) was not opened; xmlbench on sourceforge has no results text.

name: Jansson
workload: nativejson-benchmark: parse three JSON files (canada.json 2199 KB, citm_catalog.json 1737 KB, twitter.json 632 KB) into each library's DOM, and stringify the DOM back to JSON; total time over the three files.
claimed_speedup: No claim by the project; figures are from the independent suite's committed sample CSV (Jansson v2.7). Stringify total 69.9 ms vs JsonCpp 94.3 ms (1.35x) and Nlohmann 87.7 ms (1.25x), ratios derived from page data; Jansson is faster on each file (canada 64.2 vs JsonCpp 84.4 / Nlohmann 76.3 ms; citm 3.76 vs 5.68 / 7.18 ms; twitter 1.93 vs 4.14 / 4.24 ms). Parse total 112.1 ms vs JsonCpp 165.5 ms (1.48x derived) and json-c 134.6 ms (1.20x derived), but that rests on canada.json (78.5 vs JsonCpp 142.5 ms); Jansson is slower than JsonCpp on citm (22.7 vs 14.6 ms) and twitter (10.9 vs 8.5 ms) and slower than Nlohmann 2.0.3 on parse (72.5 ms total).
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0, 64-bit macOS; premake5 release configuration with optimize Full and -march=native (build/premake5.lua)
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Intel Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80GHz
tradeoffs: Mutable, reference-counted tree: every node is individually allocated (224,392 allocations for canada.json, 111,230 for citm_catalog.json, 43,822 for twitter.json in the CSV), strings are copied and object entries are kept in a hashtable (ludocode benchmark reports key reordering); in return it supports editing and re-encoding documents, full UTF-8 handling, detailed error positions and a stable C API with no dependencies.
caveats: Jansson makes no speed claim; this is a derived win in an independent suite. Results are from 2016 with Jansson v2.7 and JsonCpp 1.0.0 (current releases are far newer), on one macOS machine. The same suite shows Jansson parse far behind RapidJSON (7.9 ms total), cJSON (24.7 ms), Nlohmann 2.0.3 (72.5 ms) and others, and json-c stringifies much faster (30.8 ms total vs Jansson 69.9 ms). The independent ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks (GCC 5.3.0, -O3 -flto, Jansson 2.7) puts Jansson last in nearly every speed test: tree parse 105.18 us vs YAJL 99.31 us and RapidJSON in-situ 10.58 us, encode 63.40 us vs YAJL 37.86 us; its author calls Jansson 'even slower than YAJL'. Treat Jansson as a feature-rich mutable-tree library, not a fast one.

name: jbson
workload: JSON text parsing: mloskot/json_benchmark (1000 iterations of 500 small documents, and 1000 iterations of canada.json as one large document) and sanSS/json-bechmarks (small, medium and large objects, average time per parse and memory), jbson parsing JSON into its BSON document.
claimed_speedup: json_benchmark, README figures: large 43.0072 to 43.0377 s vs jsoncpp 62.7781 to 62.7823 s (1.46x), QJsonDocument 58.1027 to 58.1235 s (1.35x), jsoncons 243.634 to 243.796 s (5.7x); small 1.24328 to 1.27775 s vs jsoncpp 2.4124 to 2.45696 s (about 1.9x) and jsoncons 10.2386 to 10.2747 s (8x), ratios derived from page data. sanSS benchmark: medium 64,800 us vs jsoncpp 121,035 us and QJsonDocument 82,839 us; large 190,883 us vs jsoncpp 438,745 us (QJsonDocument did not finish); memory 24,708 K vs jsoncpp 44,224 K on medium objects and 1,132 K vs 4,084 K on small. README: 'it's 2nd only to rapidjson (or 3rd to QJsonDocument with small input)'.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++14 library whose JSON parser emits a BSON-style byte document that is read lazily through iterators and constant wrappers, not an in-memory DOM; BSON names cannot hold NUL so JSON compliance is partial; the README says it needs a current libc++ (codecvt and C++14 aliases missing from older libstdc++).
caveats: First-party run: the README gives the author's own timings with no compiler, flags, hardware or library versions, so tier C even though mloskot/json_benchmark is public (its own README, which lists no jbson row, shows different absolute times on other hardware). It is slower than RapidJSON (small 0.454 to 0.486 s, large 4.857 to 4.863 s, so about 9x on large) and, on small input, slower than QJsonDocument (1.046 to 1.056 s). Parsing to a lazily read BSON buffer is a different data model from the DOMs it is compared with. README's large-object memory figure is garbled ('70,7748 K'). 2015 numbers, repository last changed 2015-12-20. Both benchmark repos are unmaintained or superseded by nativejson-benchmark, which has no jbson row.
